blocks.text: READING ARCHAEOLOGY, INSCRIPTIONS AND THE BIBLICAL RECORD
From discovery to history.
The object survives. The argument begins.

How does a surviving object become a historical conclusion? Learn to distinguish preserved wording from restored letters, an excavated sequence from a calendar date, and a useful parallel from direct attestation. Six discoveries provide worked examples of how historians read evidence relating to the biblical world.
Illustrative monument and layers · not a particular find, script or excavation
01 / FROM DISCOVERY TO HISTORICAL ARGUMENT · 701 BCE
A city falls. Its story travels.
Lachish was attacked in Judah. Its capture was celebrated on a palace wall in Nineveh.

That distance is the beginning of the inquiry. The king’s image, the city’s damaged remains and the written accounts preserve different parts of the campaign. Following them together shows how a discovery becomes useful: first understand what it is, then ask what it can support.
LOOK AT THE SURVIVING OBJECT / NINEVEH
The victory the palace audience saw

This is part of the Lachish relief series, now in the British Museum. It depicts captives, the royal audience and the Assyrian camp. Select a part of the photograph to examine how the monument tells its story.
Part of the relief series, photographed in its modern museum display. Photograph: Shadsluiter · CC BY-SA 4.0. Resized; detail views crop the same photograph.
Detail / People led away
READ THE IMAGE’S PERSPECTIVE
A victory for the king. Displacement for the defeated.

The relief sequence includes captives and the spoils of Lachish. People appear within a story of royal success: the palace audience sees the power of Assyria and the submission of its enemies. For a historian, the same scene also raises questions about displacement and the people whose own accounts have not survived.
A carved procession cannot tell us the experience of every inhabitant. Its arrangement is the artist’s and patron’s presentation of victory.
From the commemorated victory to the place where the assault happened
RETURN TO THE GROUND / LACHISH
A different record of the same assault
At the city, the ramp and the destruction context can be investigated separately from the king’s account. The relationship between outside, wall and inside is the important thing to see.
The attackers changed the terrain.

The siege ramp at Lachish brought an assault up towards the city’s defences. Unlike the palace relief, it survives at the attacked place. It records engineering and labour in material form, even though it cannot supply a diary of who built it or how each stage of the assault unfolded.
Conceptual outside/inside section. Not a measured profile, stratigraphic record or reconstruction of particular wall dates. The destruction area is a teaching symbol for the archaeological context.
READ THE SURVIVING ACCOUNTS
The campaign is also an argument in words.
Written sources add named places, rulers and explanations. Their purpose still shapes what they tell us.
AKKADIAN TEXT
A king claims conquest
Sennacherib’s inscription claims the capture of forty-six fortified towns of Hezekiah and describes confining him in Jerusalem. It does not claim Jerusalem’s capture in this account.
Forty-six is an attributed royal tally, not an independently excavated count. Silence about capture is not an explanation of deliverance.
HEBREW LITERARY ACCOUNT
Kings narrates devastation and deliverance
Kings reports the loss of fortified towns, tribute sent to Sennacherib at Lachish, and Jerusalem’s deliverance. Its narrative makes prophetic speech and divine action central.
The story supplies an interpretation of survival. Material agreement on Judah’s devastation does not independently test every speech or theological explanation.
Illustrative document forms, not prism or manuscript facsimiles.
WHAT THIS FIRST CASE TEACHES
Different evidence can meet at one event without answering every question about it.

The palace image and the excavated city support a historical account of Lachish’s capture from different contexts. The relief and royal annals share an Assyrian royal setting, so their agreement does not make them fully independent witnesses. And Lachish’s fall is a different question from Jerusalem’s survival.
FOLLOW A QUESTION FURTHER
AN ARGUMENT THAT CHANGED
The fire did not come with a date attached.
Stratigraphy establishes order. A calendar date requires a further argument.
Schematic relative sequence; no measured strata, wall dates or deposits represented.
Three moments in the research, arranged in reading order. Spacing does not represent elapsed time.
EARLIER EXCAVATIONS
Two competing dates

Starkey assigned Level III to 597 BCE. Olga Tufnell instead argued for 701 when preparing the excavation publication. Identifying a burnt city was only the beginning; scholars disagreed over which destruction it represented.
RENEWED EXCAVATIONS · 1973–1977
The sequence narrowed the options

Ussishkin reported repeated checks through the strata: Level III was the fortified, fire-destroyed candidate for the eighth-century catastrophe; Level IV’s defences continued into it. The case depended on relationships between layers, not a single spectacular find.
FOURTH EXPEDITION · REPORT 2021
A correction within the reconstruction

Garfinkel and colleagues reassigned the lower “revetment” wall to the Middle Bronze Age using its relationship to a later fortress. They retained the Level III/701 association. Revising the age of one wall need not overturn the identification of the whole campaign.
02 / THE WIDER COLLECTION
What can an object establish?
Six selected cases, not a complete inventory. Inspect a detail before judging the claim.
Six selected cases. Object silhouettes and surface guide lines are illustrative, not facsimiles; size does not represent dimensions or historical importance.
Selected discovery: Merneptah stele
CASE 01 / THEBES · EGYPT
When does Israel enter the external written record?
Granite victory stele Egyptian · hieroglyphs
Merneptah stele
Near the end of an Egyptian victory hymn, Israel appears among the defeated. The boast preserves a name even as it announces destruction.
Granite victory stele · Egyptian · hieroglyphs
Joshua narrates Israel’s campaigns and possession of land. The stele supplies a separate Egyptian reference to Israel; it does not identify Joshua or describe his campaigns.
Contextual comparison, not the same narrated event. Biblical narrative and royal victory hymn have different purposes.
Contemporary royal testimony about Merneptah’s victories; an external chronological anchor for a people, not an eyewitness record of the biblical origin story.
CLOSE READING / MERNEPTAH STELE
Inspect the wording & details
INSPECT THE EVIDENCE / THE FINAL VICTORY STANZA
“the people of Israel is laid waste, their crops are not”
Short extract · UCL translation
A name is a chronological anchor.

The important discovery is the name’s presence in an Egyptian royal composition. It places a group called Israel within the writer’s Canaanite horizon by Merneptah’s fifth year. It does not describe that group’s arrival.
Establishes
By the late thirteenth century BCE, an Egyptian royal text names Israel in its account of Canaan. The writing classifies Israel as a people, unlike the place names beside it.
Suggests
Israel was a recognizable social group to Egyptian scribes. That constrains histories of Israel’s emergence, but gives neither a population count nor a map of its territory.
Unresolved
The inscription cannot identify an Exodus pharaoh, date the Exodus, or establish Joshua’s conquest sequence. Its language of devastation is a victory claim, not a demographic survey.
03 / READ THE LETTERS AND THE GAPS
Three different kinds of uncertainty.
A missing letter, a disputed mark and a proposed join are different problems. Treating all of them as simply “uncertain” conceals how epigraphers work.
Brackets do not mean “anything could go here”.
Surviving letters, Latin grammar and official terminology constrain the restoration. The name and office are more secure than the damaged dedication’s architectural purpose.
Portions of lines 2–3, in transcription. Brackets identify editorial supplements; spacing and line lengths do not reproduce the stone.
Pontius Pilate · prefect of Judaea
02 / MESHA · CONTESTED MARKS
Are the marks letters, damage or folds?

Reflectance Transformation Imaging (RTI) combines photographs lit from different directions to help inspect a surface. A squeeze is a paper impression. Both improve access to marks; neither interprets those marks automatically. Taw and dalet are letter names; a word divider is a separating mark.
Method illustration, not Mesha’s surface or a simulation of disputed marks.
HOW THE SURFACE BECOMES VISIBLE
One surface. Multiple directions of light.
RTI combines photographs taken under different lighting directions. It helps examine surface relief; it does not decide whether a trace is a letter.
Lemaire & Delorme
Lemaire and Delorme compare faint traces with the size and orientation of taw elsewhere on the stele.
Richelle & Burlingame
Richelle and Burlingame question whether the supposed strokes are deliberate cuts rather than surface irregularities.

The dispute concerns the identification of particular marks, not whether David matters to the reader. House of David remains a disputed reading here; Tel Dan is a separate, stronger attestation. “Uncertain” does not make every imaginable completion equally plausible.
03 / TEL DAN · A PROPOSED JOIN
What if the fragments do not continue the same lines?

Langlois (2024) argues that A and B differ systematically in letter execution and lack a secure physical join. He proposes placing them elsewhere, possibly on related monuments. Further physical and contextual study is required.
Textual argument diagram, not shapes, spacing or placement of the real fragments. The dashed connection represents an editorial proposal.
The words “king of Israel” and BYTDWD remain on fragment A in either arrangement. The larger narrative becomes less secure; the surviving phrase does not disappear.
04 / TEST A HISTORICAL PARALLEL
A restorer of sanctuaries. Whose sanctuaries?
A parallel becomes useful when the differences stay visible. Read these summaries of the two texts, then test the connection.
Cyrus Cylinder Marduk → Cyrus → Babylon
Ezra The LORD → Cyrus → Jerusalem
Illustrative document forms. Labels summarize the selected comparison; they are not quotations or manuscript facsimiles.
Cyrus Cylinder
Marduk selects Cyrus and leads him to Babylon (lines 12–17).
Ezra
The LORD stirs Cyrus and commissions a house in Jerusalem (Ezra 1:1–2).
Both connect kingship with divine purpose. Identifying a comparable form of royal legitimation does not identify the gods or theological claims with one another.
Context, not a duplicate decree.

Cyrus’s restoration rhetoric makes Ezra historically intelligible within imperial practice. It does not independently authenticate Ezra’s decree. Nor is the cylinder a universal declaration of equal rights in the modern sense.

Kuhrt’s 1983 study is a foundational point of departure for this question. Van der Spek’s later comparison places restoration beside earlier Assyrian and Babylonian practices. That comparison asks what is distinctive about Cyrus rather than assuming a completely new policy.
05 / TRY THE DISTINCTION
How far can this claim go?
Question 1 of 3
Illustrative object form
“The Cyrus Cylinder is the decree to Jerusalem quoted in Ezra.”
06 / ENTER THE SCHOLARLY CONVERSATION
Follow an argument, not just a bibliography.
Excavation, epigraphy and historical interpretation answer different questions. These works show how the questions themselves changed.
Read the ground
Read the surface
Read the world around it
SELECTED RESEARCH PATH / 01
Tufnell’s alternative, tested by Ussishkin

Read Ussishkin’s 1978 account of the Level III debate, then pursue the 2004 excavation volumes. The sequence shows why publishing deposits and checking stratigraphy can change a historical identification.
Whose history survives?

This selection travels through Egypt, Moab, Aram, Judah, Babylonia and Roman Judaea, across Egyptian, Moabite, Aramaic, Akkadian and Latin texts. These are distinct scholarly fields and ancient perspectives. None is merely a caption to a biblical story.

Royal monuments disproportionately preserve conquest and public authority. Storage vessels, domestic contexts and regional settlement patterns ask other questions: who produced, supplied, rebuilt and endured? The survival of a king’s words is not a measure of whose life mattered most.
SOURCE REGISTER / ACCESS & LIMITATIONS
Follow the evidence past this page.
This is a curated selection, not a catalogue of “proofs”. Royal monuments preserve powerful voices; ordinary lives are less evenly represented.

Research expanded 14 October 2026. Catalogue descriptions, primary texts, scholarly reconstructions and our teaching inferences are distinguished throughout. The relief photograph is attributed beside its display; other object artwork is illustrative.
A discovery becomes more useful when its limits become clearer.
